extracted.intended_audience: USCIS/DHS adjudicators, immigration attorneys, consular officers, and other immigration practitioners and policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural criteria governing public-charge inadmissibility determinations, related evidentiary requirements for adjustment of status (including T nonimmigrants), and related regulatory definitions and procedural references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public charge bond procedures (8 CFR 103.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: All public charge bonds are subject to the procedures established in 8 CFR 103.6 relating to bond riders, acceptable sureties, cancellation of bonds, and breach of bonds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the procedural rules in 8 CFR 103.6 when handling public charge bonds (including riders, acceptable sureties, cancellation, breach).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inadmissibility under section 212(a) and waiver requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: An alien is inadmissible under any applicable provisions of section 212(a) of the Act and has not obtained a waiver of inadmissibility in accordance with 8 CFR 212.18 or 214.11(j).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before approving adjustment of status, adjudicators must determine whether any section 212(a) ground renders the alien inadmissible and verify whether a statutory/regulatory waiver under 8 CFR 212.18 or 214.11(j) has been obtained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Victimization exception for unlawful presence (T nonimmigrants)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the alien establishes that the victimization was a central reason for the alien's unlawful presence in the United States, section 212(a)(9)(B)(iii) of the Act is not applicable, and the alien need not obtain a waiver of that ground of inadmissibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To qualify for this exception the alien must submit with Form I-485 evidence sufficient to demonstrate that the victimization suffered was a central reason for the unlawful presence. The victimization need not be the sole reason, but the nexus between the victimization and the unlawful presence must be more than tangential, incidental, or superficial.

rubrics_metrics.name: List of public benefits relevant to public-charge determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2019 Final Rule designated a specific list of public benefits as relevant to the public charge determination, including benefits beyond cash assistance for income maintenance and long-term institutionalization at government expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of benefits identified as relevant in prior rulemaking include SNAP, most non-emergency forms of Medicaid, Section 8 Housing Assistance under the Housing Choice Voucher (HCV) Program, Section 8 Project-Based Rental Assistance, and public housing under the Housing Act of 1937. Adjudicators should consider this enumerated list (and any updates) when assessing public-benefit receipt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit of Support requirement (Form I-864 / I-864EZ)
rubrics_metrics.description: When required, the applicant must submit an Affidavit of Support Under Section 213A of the INA (Form I-864 or Form I-864EZ). With very limited exceptions, most noncitizens seeking family-based immigrant visas and adjustment of status, and some noncitizens seeking employment-based immigrant visas or adjustment of status, must submit a sufficient Affidavit of Support in order to avoid being found inadmissible as likely at any time to become a public charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify receipt and sufficiency of Form I-864/I-864EZ when applicable; note the limited statutory exceptions and that failure to provide a required affidavit may result in inadmissibility as likely to become a public charge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory exemptions from public-charge ground
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress has by statute exempted certain categories of noncitizens, such as asylees and refugees, from the public charge ground of inadmissibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check statutory exemptions listed in the rule and applicable statutes (e.g., INA secs. 207(c)(3), 209(c)) to determine whether an applicant falls within an exempt category before applying the public-charge ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory definitions and specific guidance (8 CFR 212.21; 212.22)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations provide definitions for key terms (including 'receipt (of public benefits)' and 'household') and specific guidance (e.g., treatment of disabilities) in 8 CFR 212.21 and 8 CFR 212.22.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjudicators must apply the definitional and procedural guidance in 8 CFR 212.21 and 8 CFR 212.22 (including any subsections addressing disabilities or other special considerations) when making public-charge determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Student financial support documentary requirement (8 CFR 214.1 / 214.2; AFM)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students (F, M, J categories where applicable) must present documentary evidence of financial support in the amount indicated on the SEVIS Form I-20 (or corresponding forms); AFM guidance requires applicants to demonstrate financial resources to pay for coursework and living expenses when changing status to a student.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consular officers and adjudicators should require and evaluate documentary proof of sufficient funds (per 8 CFR 214.1(f)(1)(i)(B), 214.2(m)(1)(i)(B), AFM Chapter 30.3(c)(2)(C), and related DOS regs) before approving student visas or changes of status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nexus/standard of proof for central-reason showing
rubrics_metrics.description: The nexus between victimization and unlawful presence must be more than tangential, incidental, or superficial to qualify for the exception to section 212(a)(9)(B)(iii).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjudicators must assess the sufficiency of evidence submitted with Form I-485 to determine whether the victimization was a central reason (not merely tangential or incidental) for unlawful presence; evaluate factual narratives, corroborating documentation, and temporal connection to unlawful presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive approaches to 'public charge' (historical and judicial standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial interpretations of 'public charge' vary: some courts and historical practice equate it to long-term dependence for survival, while other authorities read it more broadly to include receipt of certain government assistance or an obligation imposed on the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal analysis and adjudication should account for divergent case law and historical evolution of the term; DHS recognizes ambiguity and asserts regulatory interpretation within the Executive's delegated discretion, but adjudicators should be familiar with relevant precedents (e.g., Cook County v. Wolf; New York v. DHS; City & County of San Francisco v. USCIS) when applying the standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of statutory grounds absent implementing regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: The vast majority of the grounds of inadmissibility at section 212 of the INA have not been implemented by regulation, but are administered and enforced by DHS based on the statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjudicators and practitioners must remember that absence of a specific implementing regulation does not preclude application of a statutory inadmissibility ground; statutory text and governing case law control where regulations do not exist.
